title: WHAT WAS PAUL’S THORN IN THE FLESH? THE ANSWER MAY BE MORE PERSONAL THAN YOU THINK
paragraphs: WHAT WAS PAUL’S THORN IN THE FLESH? THE ANSWER MAY BE MORE PERSONAL THAN YOU THINK
Paul begged Jesus three times to take it away.
Jesus didn’t.
And perhaps the most unsettling part of the story is that Paul never tells us exactly what “it” was.
For nearly two thousand years, Christians have wondered about those mysterious words buried inside one of the most vulnerable passages the apostle Paul ever wrote.
Was it sickness?
Problems with his eyesight?
Persecution?
Temptation?
Depression?
A physical disability?
A demonic attack?
An enemy who continually opposed his ministry?
Something else entirely?
People have proposed all of these possibilities.
But Scripture does something fascinating.
It leaves the thorn unnamed.
And maybe before asking, “What exactly was Paul’s thorn?” we need to notice something even more important.
Paul tells us what the thorn did.
He tells us where it came against him.
He tells us how desperately he wanted it gone.
And then he tells us what Jesus said when the thorn stayed.
That is where this ancient mystery suddenly becomes painfully personal.
Because somewhere in your life, you may have something you have asked God to remove too.
Something you thought would be gone by now.
Something you prayed about when nobody was listening.
Something you have cried over.
Something you have rebuked.
Something you have surrendered.
Something you have asked God to heal, change, stop, restore, or take away.
And yet...
it remains.
So you started wondering whether God had forgotten you.
Paul knew that prayer.
Listen carefully to his own language.
In 2 Corinthians 12:7, the Greek text says:
“ἐδόθη μοι σκόλοψ τῇ σαρκί, ἄγγελος Σατανᾶ, ἵνα με κολαφίζῃ”
Transliterated:
“edothē moi skolops tē sarki, angelos Satana, hina me kolaphizē.”
A close rendering is:
“There was given to me a thorn in the flesh, a messenger of Satan, that it might buffet/strike me.”
The word translated “thorn” is σκόλοψ — skolops.
And this matters.
We often imagine a tiny rose thorn stuck beneath somebody’s skin.

Paul’s word can carry the sense of something pointed, sharp, even stake-like. Whatever Paul experienced, his imagery was not describing a cute inconvenience. It communicated something piercing and deeply distressing.
Then Paul uses another violent word.
κολαφίζῃ — kolaphizē.
It carries the idea of striking or buffeting, even striking with the fist.
Paul was not saying, “God gave me a mildly annoying problem.”
He was describing something that battered him.
Something humiliating.
Something persistent.
Something he desperately wanted gone.
And Scripture explicitly calls it “ἄγγελος Σατανᾶ” — angelos Satana — “a messenger of Satan.”
Yet here is where we must be careful.
Paul does not explicitly tell us what physical form or circumstance that messenger produced.
That silence matters.

Some interpreters throughout Christian history have suggested a physical illness. Others have connected the thorn with Paul’s bodily weakness or possible problems involving his eyes. Others have argued for persecution, hostile opponents, spiritual assault, or another form of suffering.
There are arguments for different possibilities.
But none of them should be preached as though Paul wrote, “My thorn was ______.”
He didn't.
The inspired text gives us boundaries.
It was a “thorn in the flesh.”
It was associated with a “messenger of Satan.”
It “buffeted” Paul.
It was severe enough that Paul repeatedly pleaded for its removal.
And it served, under God's sovereign providence, to keep Paul from becoming exalted because of the extraordinary revelations he had received.
Beyond that, certainty becomes speculation.
And perhaps that is exactly where many sermons go wrong.
We become obsessed with identifying Paul's thorn while overlooking the words Jesus actually wanted Paul to remember.
Because Paul prayed.
Once.
The thorn remained.
Paul prayed again.
Still there.
Then again.
Three times.
“Lord...
take this away.”
Imagine Paul praying that.
The apostle who saw Christ.
The missionary through whom churches were planted.
The man who preached Christ when preaching Christ could get him beaten, imprisoned, or killed.
Paul knew miracles.
Paul knew deliverance.
Paul knew supernatural power.
Paul had watched God do extraordinary things.
And still there was something in Paul's own life that would not leave when he asked.
That should destroy one dangerous idea immediately:
Unanswered prayer does not automatically mean you lack faith.
Sometimes enormous faith is found in the person who keeps trusting Jesus after the answer they wanted never arrives.
Paul says:
“ὑπὲρ τούτου τρὶς τὸν Κύριον παρεκάλεσα”
“Concerning this, three times I pleaded with the Lord...”
He wasn't casual.
He pleaded.
Take it away.
Take it away.
Please...
take it away.
And then Jesus answered.
But Jesus did not answer the way Paul requested.
He said:
“Ἀρκεῖ σοι ἡ χάρις μου.”
Arkei soi hē charis mou.
“My grace is sufficient for you.”
Read that again.
Not:
“My explanation is sufficient for you.”
Not:
“Your strength is sufficient.”
Not:
“Try harder.”
Not:
“Pretend this doesn't hurt.”
Not even:
“I will remove it tomorrow.”
“My grace is sufficient for you.”
Then comes the sentence that completely rewrites the meaning of weakness:
“For My power is perfected in weakness.”
This is Christianity in a sentence that human pride would never invent.
We want power without weakness.
Christ reveals power through weakness.
We want victory without scars.
Jesus conquered through a cross.
We want resurrection without death.
But the Gospel takes us straight through Calvary before it shows us the empty tomb.
And suddenly Paul's thorn begins pointing beyond Paul.
It points toward Christ.
Paul was learning that the Christian life is not ultimately the story of how impressive Paul could become.
It is the story of how sufficient Christ already is.
That changes everything.
Because perhaps you have been measuring God's love by what He removes.
Paul learned to recognize Christ's power even in what remained.
That does not mean suffering is good in itself.
It does not mean Satan becomes good.
It does not mean sickness, persecution, grief, temptation, trauma, or affliction should be romanticized.
And it certainly does not mean Christians should refuse medicine, counseling, protection, justice, wise help, or prayer for healing.
Paul himself asked for deliverance.
Three times.
There is nothing faithless about asking Jesus to remove the thorn.
Ask Him.
Cry before Him.
Seek help.
Pray boldly.
Call the elders.
Seek healing.
Seek wisdom.
Seek freedom.
But do not make this mistake:
Do not assume that because the thorn has not disappeared, Jesus has disappeared.
Paul discovered something astonishing.
The thorn could remain...
and Christ could remain closer.
The weakness could remain...
and Christ's power could remain greater.
The unanswered question could remain...
and grace could still be enough.
Maybe that is why Scripture never gives us Paul's medical chart.
Maybe God knew generations of wounded Christians would eventually read this passage.
The exhausted mother praying over a child.
The husband staring at a marriage he cannot repair by himself.
The believer fighting the same temptation again.
The pastor preaching while privately exhausted.
The Christian living with chronic pain.
The person carrying grief everybody assumes they should have “gotten over” already.
The believer asking God at 2:13 in the morning:
“Why hasn't this changed?”
You read Paul's story wanting the name of his thorn.
Then somewhere between verse seven and verse nine...
you realize you have been thinking about yours.
And that may be where this passage catches the soul.
Because some of us have secretly made God a bargain.
“Lord, once You fix this, I'll finally have peace.”
“Once You heal this, I'll trust You.”
“Once You restore this relationship, I'll worship again.”
“Once You remove this weakness, then You can use me.”
Paul's testimony destroys that bargain.
Christ can use you while you are weak.
Christ can sustain you while you are hurting.
Christ can humble you without abandoning you.
Christ can display His strength through places you desperately wish were stronger.
And sometimes the place you are most ashamed of becomes the place where you finally stop pretending you can save yourself.
That is Gospel territory.
Because the deepest thorn in humanity is not Paul's mysterious affliction.
It is sin.
And Jesus did not come merely to make uncomfortable people comfortable.
He came to save sinners.
Paul himself once stood on the scandalous side of that story.
Before Christians knew him as the apostle Paul, they feared him as Saul.
He approved Stephen's death.
He ravaged the church.
He dragged believers away.
He breathed threats against the disciples of Jesus.
Then Christ met him.
The persecutor became the preacher.
The enemy became the apostle.
The man who once tried to silence the name of Jesus eventually suffered to proclaim it.
That is scandal becoming grace.
Not because Paul's past became innocent.
Grace does not rewrite evil by pretending it never happened.
Jesus rewrites the sinner's future by forgiving, redeeming, transforming, and claiming those who come to Him.
Paul would never again be merely “the man who persecuted Christians.”
He became living evidence that the mercy of Christ can reach people whose histories look impossible to redeem.
And years later, that redeemed man was still weak.
Think about that.
Grace had transformed Paul.
Grace had not made Paul invulnerable.
He still needed Jesus.
Maybe you needed to hear that.
Spiritual maturity is not reaching the point where you no longer need grace.
Spiritual maturity is discovering how desperately you have always needed it.
Paul eventually says something almost shocking:
He will boast in his weaknesses so that the power of Christ may rest upon him.
Not because pain suddenly feels wonderful.
Because Christ has become more precious than the illusion of self-sufficiency.
That is the real revelation of the thorn.
The great mystery is not what was stabbing Paul.
The great revelation is what was sustaining him.
Jesus.
Jesus was enough.
And if you are reading this while carrying something you desperately wish God would remove, I will not insult your suffering by telling you it doesn't hurt.
Paul never did that.
Call the thorn a thorn.
Cry.
Pray.
Ask God for deliverance.
But while you wait...
do not confuse God's silence with God's absence.
Do not confuse weakness with uselessness.
Do not confuse suffering with rejection.
And do not allow the enemy to convince you that your unfinished battle disqualifies you from coming to Christ.
Come weak.
Come wounded.
Come ashamed.
Come exhausted.
Come with the prayer you have already prayed a hundred times.
Come with your sins exposed.
Come with nothing impressive left to offer.
Jesus did not die for a polished version of you.
Christ died for sinners.

He bore sin upon the cross, died, was buried, and rose again. Forgiveness is not earned through religious performance. Salvation is God's grace received through faith in Jesus Christ, producing a life turned toward Him in repentance and obedience.
Maybe your greatest need today is not discovering Paul's thorn.
Maybe it is finally admitting yours.
The hidden sin.
The pride.
The bitterness.
The secret addiction.
The resentment.
The exhaustion.
The fear.
The wound.
The prayer that seems unanswered.
The thing behind the Christian smile nobody sees.
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
If something hidden has been exposed, comment, “Jesus, forgive me.”
If you cannot even explain what you're carrying anymore, simply comment, “Pray for me.”
Someone scrolling beneath you may desperately need evidence that grace still reaches people in dark places.
No pretending.
No Christian masks.
Just people who need Jesus pointing one another toward Jesus.
And please don't let this article die on your screen.
Not because sharing a post earns God's favor—it absolutely does not—but because someone connected to you may be quietly asking the same question Paul asked.
“Lord, why won't this leave?”
Your share could place Scripture in front of somebody at precisely the moment they need it.
Send this to the believer who thinks weakness means God cannot use them.
“Ἀρκεῖ σοι ἡ χάρις μου.”
“My grace is sufficient for you.”
Supporting Christian ministry does not purchase God's blessing, prove salvation, or make someone more righteous before Him. Jesus cannot be bought. Grace cannot be purchased.
But generosity can help Gospel-centered resources continue being created, distributed, and placed before people who need them.
But before you leave, remember Paul.
He asked for the thorn to disappear.
Christ gave him something greater than an explanation.
Grace.
Perhaps one day God will remove the thing you have been begging Him to remove.
Perhaps He will answer differently than you imagined.
But either way, the Christian's final hope was never a thornless life.
Our hope is the crucified and risen Christ.
The Savior whose own body carried wounds.
The King who turns persecutors into apostles.
The Redeemer who turns shame into testimony.
The Lord who takes sinners headed toward judgment and clothes them in a righteousness they could never manufacture for themselves.
And the Christ who can look into the weakest place of your life and say:
“My grace is sufficient for you.”
So what was Paul's thorn?
Scripture does not finally tell us.
And perhaps that unanswered question leaves us staring at the answer that matters most.
Paul's thorn had a mystery.
Paul's Savior did not.
His name is Jesus.
And sometimes Jesus does not remove the chapter you desperately wanted erased—He enters it, covers it with grace, and makes even your weakness tell the world who carried you.
